docs.title: obs -- Your Vault's Command Line
docs.text:
A laser-focused CLI for Obsidian vault management with AI-powered graph analysis.

Install Now Quick Reference

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
Vault Discovery

Automatically find and scan Obsidian vaults. Tracks notes, links, tags, and graph structure in a local SQLite database.

AI Insights

Find similar notes, detect duplicates, identify knowledge gaps, and get reorganization suggestions -- powered by 5 AI providers with smart fallback routing.

Graph Analysis

PageRank, centrality, clustering, orphan/hub detection. Understand your vault's structure at a glance with the health dashboard.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# 1. Install
brew install data-wise/tap/obsidian-cli-ops

# 2. Discover your vaults
obs discover ~/Documents --scan

# 3. Check vault health
obs health MyVault

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Obsidian CLI Ops includes AI-powered features for:

  • Note Similarity Detection - Find similar notes using semantic embeddings
  • Duplicate Detection - Identify potential duplicate notes automatically
  • Topic Analysis - Extract topics and themes from your vault
  • Smart Recommendations - Get suggestions for note organization and merging

docs.title: Privacy First
docs.text: All AI options are 100% free and run locally on your machine. No data is sent to external servers, and there are no API costs.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
The fastest way to get started is with Quick Start mode:

obs ai setup --quick

This will:

  1. ✅ Auto-detect your system capabilities
  2. ✅ Recommend the best AI provider for your setup
  3. ✅ Install and configure everything automatically
  4. ✅ Test the installation to verify it works
  5. ✅ Save your configuration

Time: ~5 minutes on first run (downloads models)

docs.title: Detailed Setup
docs.text:
For more control over your setup, use interactive mode:

obs ai setup

You'll be presented with two paths:

docs.title: Path 1: Quick Start (Recommended)
docs.text:
Best for: - First-time users - Users who want "it just works" - Users with typical setups

What it does: - Detects if Ollama is installed and running - Detects if Python packages are already installed - Recommends the best option based on your system - Installs and tests automatically

Typical recommendation: - If Ollama is running → Use Ollama - If sentence-transformers installed → Use HuggingFace - Otherwise → Install HuggingFace (most compatible)

docs.title: Path 2: Custom Setup
docs.text:
Best for: - Tech-savvy users - Users with specific requirements - Users who want to choose models

What you can customize: - AI provider (HuggingFace or Ollama) - Model size and quality - Performance vs. quality tradeoffs

docs.title: Provider Comparison
docs.text: Feature HuggingFace ⭐ Ollama Cost FREE forever FREE forever Privacy 100% local 100% local Setup Easy (pip install) Medium (requires Ollama) Dependencies Python only Ollama service Speed Medium Fast (with small models) Quality Good Good to Excellent Embeddings ✅ 384-1024 dim ✅ 768 dim Reasoning ❌ ✅ (with chat models) Offline ✅ Yes ✅ Yes RAM Usage 500MB - 2GB 500MB - 5GB Best For Most users Power users

docs.title: HuggingFace (Recommended)
docs.text:
Pros: - Pure Python, no external services - Works everywhere (Mac, Linux, Windows) - Free forever (no quotas, no limits) - Easy to install (pip install sentence-transformers) - Multiple model sizes to choose from

Cons: - Slower than Ollama for batch processing - No built-in reasoning capabilities - Models take disk space (80MB - 1.3GB)

Model Options:

Model Size Dimension Speed Best For all-MiniLM-L6-v2 80MB 384 Fast Testing, small vaults all-mpnet-base-v2 ⭐ 420MB 768 Medium Production use bge-large-en-v1.5 1.3GB 1024 Slow Maximum quality

Recommended: all-mpnet-base-v2 for best balance

docs.title: Ollama
docs.text:
Pros: - Fast embedding generation - Includes reasoning capabilities (chat models) - Can use very small models (qwen2.5:0.5b = 500MB) - Active development and community - Can run models locally without Python

Cons: - Requires Ollama installation - Requires background service running - Slightly more complex setup

Installation Options:

# Option 1: Homebrew CLI (recommended)
brew install ollama

# Option 2: Homebrew Cask (GUI app)
brew install --cask ollama-app

# Option 3: Official installer
# Download from: https://ollama.com/download

After installation:

# Start Ollama service
ollama serve

# Pull recommended models (in another terminal)
ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b        # Chat model (500MB, fast)
ollama pull nomic-embed-text    # Embedding model (768-dim)

Model Options:

Model Size Speed Quality Best For qwen2.5:0.5b ⭐ 500MB Fast Good Most users llama3.1 4GB Slow Excellent Maximum quality mistral 4GB Medium Excellent Balance

Recommended: qwen2.5:0.5b for speed, llama3.1 for quality

docs.title: HuggingFace Issues
docs.text:
Problem: ImportError: No module named 'sentence_transformers'

Solution: 

pip install sentence-transformers
# or
pip3 install sentence-transformers

Problem: OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device

Solution: Models take disk space. Free up space or use a smaller model: - all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (80MB) instead of bge-large-en-v1.5 (1.3GB)

Problem: RuntimeError: Failed to load model

Solution: Clear cache and retry: 

rm -rf ~/.cache/huggingface/
obs ai setup

Problem: Slow performance on older Mac

Solution: Use the smallest model: 

# During Custom Setup, choose:
# Model: all-MiniLM-L6-v2

docs.title: Ollama Issues
docs.text:
Problem: ConnectionError: Cannot connect to Ollama

Solution: Start Ollama service: 

ollama serve

Problem: ollama: command not found

Solution: Install Ollama: 

brew install ollama

Problem: Model download fails

Solution: Check internet connection and retry: 

ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b
ollama pull nomic-embed-text

Problem: Ollama service won't start

Solution: Check if port 11434 is in use: 

lsof -i :11434
# If another process is using it, kill it:
kill -9 <PID>
# Then retry:
ollama serve

Problem: High RAM usage with llama3.1

Solution: Use smaller model: 

ollama pull qwen2.5:0.5b
# Then re-run setup and choose qwen2.5:0.5b

docs.title: General Issues
docs.text:
Problem: rich library installation fails

Solution: The setup wizard auto-installs rich, but if it fails: 

pip install rich
# or
pip3 install rich

Problem: Python 3.8 or older

Solution: Upgrade Python: 

brew install python@3.9

Problem: Setup wizard freezes

Solution: 1. Press Ctrl+C to cancel 2. Check internet connection 3. Retry with --quick flag: 

obs ai setup --quick

Problem: "Permission denied" errors

Solution: Install to user directory: 

pip install --user sentence-transformers

docs.title: Minimum Requirements
docs.text:
• OS: macOS 10.15+, Linux (most distros), Windows 10+
  • Python: 3.9 or higher
  • RAM: 4GB (8GB recommended)
  • Disk: 500MB - 2GB (depending on models)
  • Internet: Required for initial model download only

docs.title: Recommended Requirements
docs.text:
• OS: macOS 12+ (M1/M2 Macs for best performance)
  • Python: 3.10+
  • RAM: 8GB or more
  • Disk: 2GB free space
  • CPU: Apple Silicon or modern Intel/AMD

docs.title: Is this really free?
docs.text: Yes. Both HuggingFace and Ollama are 100% free and open source. There are no API costs, no quotas, and no hidden fees.

docs.title: Does my data leave my machine?
docs.text: No. Everything runs locally on your computer. Your notes never leave your machine.

docs.title: Can I use both providers?
docs.text: Not yet. Currently, you choose one provider during setup. Multi-provider support is planned for a future release.

docs.title: Which provider should I choose?
docs.text:
For most users: HuggingFace with all-mpnet-base-v2 model - Easy setup - Good performance - Free forever - Works everywhere

For power users: Ollama with qwen2.5:0.5b model - Faster processing - Reasoning capabilities - More flexibility

docs.title: Can I change my setup later?
docs.text: Yes. Just run obs ai setup again. Your previous configuration will be detected, and you can choose a new provider or model.

docs.title: How much disk space do I need?
docs.text:
HuggingFace: - Minimum: 80MB (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) - Recommended: 420MB (all-mpnet-base-v2) - Maximum: 1.3GB (bge-large-en-v1.5)

Ollama: - Minimum: 500MB (qwen2.5:0.5b) + 274MB (nomic-embed-text) - Recommended: Same as minimum - Maximum: 4GB (llama3.1) + 274MB (nomic-embed-text)

docs.title: Will this work offline?
docs.text: Yes. After initial setup and model download, everything works offline.

docs.title: Can I use my own models?
docs.text: Not yet. Custom model support is planned for a future release.

docs.title: What if I have a slow internet connection?
docs.text:
Use Quick Start with HuggingFace. The default model (all-mpnet-base-v2) is only 420MB. If your connection is very slow, you can:

  1. Use Custom Setup
  2. Choose HuggingFace
  3. Select all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (only 80MB)

docs.title: How do I uninstall?
docs.text:
HuggingFace: 

pip uninstall sentence-transformers
rm -rf ~/.cache/huggingface/
rm ~/.config/obs/ai_config.json

Ollama: 

brew uninstall ollama
# or
brew uninstall --cask ollama-app
rm ~/.config/obs/ai_config.json

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text:
You can override default settings with environment variables:

# Change config directory
export OBS_AI_CONFIG_DIR="$HOME/.my-config"

# Use specific Python
export PYTHON_BIN="/usr/local/bin/python3.11"

docs.title: Manual Configuration
docs.text:
You can manually edit the config file:

# Edit config
vim ~/.config/obs/ai_config.json

# Test configuration
obs ai config

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
You can also use the AI clients directly in Python:

from ai_client import get_ai_client

# Get HuggingFace client
client = get_ai_client("huggingface", model_name="all-mpnet-base-v2")

# Get embedding
embedding = client.get_embedding("My note content")

# Compare notes
score = client.compare_notes("Note 1 content", "Note 2 content")
print(f"Similarity: {score.score:.2f}")

docs.title: Ollama API
docs.text:
Direct Ollama API usage:

from ai_client import get_ai_client

# Get Ollama client
client = get_ai_client("ollama",
                      embedding_model="nomic-embed-text",
                      chat_model="qwen2.5:0.5b")

# Compare with reasoning
score = client.compare_notes(
    "Statistical mediation analysis",
    "Causal mediation methods",
    use_reasoning=True  # Use chat model for better comparison
)
print(f"Similarity: {score.score:.2f}")
print(f"Reason: {score.reason}")

docs.title: obs discover
docs.text:
Find Obsidian vaults in a directory tree.

obs discover <path> [--scan]
Argument Description path Root directory to search --scan Scan discovered vaults immediately

Searches for .obsidian/ directories recursively. With --scan, populates the database for each found vault.

docs.title: obs stats
docs.text:
Show vault or global statistics.

obs stats [--vault <name|id>]
Argument Description --vault Vault name or ID (full or prefix). Omit for global stats.

Examples:

obs stats                    # Global stats (all vaults)
obs stats --vault MyVault    # Specific vault stats
obs stats --vault abc        # Prefix lookup

docs.text:

  • Link Integrity -- broken link count
  • Structure -- tag coverage, hub balance
  • Freshness -- stale note detection

docs.title: Run a full health check
docs.text:
obs analyze MyVault        # Graph metrics (density, clusters)
obs health MyVault         # Health scores (4 dimensions)
obs ai gaps MyVault        # Knowledge gaps
obs ai refactor MyVault    # Reorganization plan

docs.title: Find and organize orphaned notes
docs.text:
Orphaned notes have no incoming or outgoing links. They're invisible to graph navigation.

# See orphan count
obs health MyVault

# Get AI-powered reorganization plan
obs ai refactor MyVault

# Preview scope first (no AI calls)
obs ai refactor MyVault --dry-run

What to do with orphans:

  • Link them to relevant hub notes or MOCs (Maps of Content)
  • Some orphans are fine (daily notes, templates)
  • High orphan count (>20%) suggests poor linking habits

docs.title: Archive stale folders
docs.text:
The refactor command detects folders where all notes are >90 days old with low connectivity:

obs ai refactor MyVault --json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
plan = json.load(sys.stdin)
for s in plan['suggestions']:
    if s['category'] == 'archive':
        print(f\"Archive: {s['affected_paths']}\")
"

docs.title: Consolidate small folders
docs.text:
Folders with fewer than 3 notes are flagged for merging:

obs ai refactor MyVault --json | python3 -c "
import json, sys
plan = json.load(sys.stdin)
for s in plan['suggestions']:
    if s['category'] == 'merge-folder':
        print(s['description'])
"

docs.title: Understand graph density
docs.text:

Density Interpretation < 0.01 Sparse -- many isolated notes 0.01-0.05 Typical -- healthy vault 0.05-0.10 Dense -- well-connected > 0.10 Very dense -- may have over-linking

Hub notes are the backbone of your knowledge graph. Review them regularly -- they influence many notes. Consider splitting hubs with 50+ connections.

docs.title: Understand clusters
docs.text:
Clusters are groups of notes more connected to each other than to the rest. The cluster count in obs analyze output tells you how many topic communities exist:

  • Very few clusters (1-2): vault may lack structure
  • Many small clusters: topics may not be cross-linked enough
  • Each cluster typically represents a topic or project

Recommended Alternative:

  path <- fs::path(vault_path, "R-Notes", paste0(Sys.Date(), ".md"))
  writeLines(content, path)
  message("✓ Written to Obsidian: ", path)
}

docs.title: R-Dev Integration
docs.text: The r-dev module connects your R/Emacs workflow to your Obsidian "Lab Notebook".

docs.title: 1. Link a Project
docs.text:
Tell obs where this R project lives in your vault.

cd ~/projects/RMediation
obs r-dev link Research_Lab/RMediation_Package

This creates a mapping in ~/.config/obs/project_map.json so future commands auto-detect the correct Obsidian folder.

docs.title: 2. Check Status (Optional)
docs.text:
See if the current R project is linked.

obs r-dev status

Shows: - R project root path - Mapped Obsidian folder - Whether the mapping exists

docs.title: 3. Log Results
docs.text:
Push simulation plots or HTML reports to the 06_Analysis folder.

obs r-dev log results/plot.png -m "Sensitivity analysis n=500"

Files are automatically timestamped to prevent overwrites.

docs.title: 4. Fetch Theory
docs.text:
Grab mathematical context from your Knowledge Base while coding.

obs r-dev context "Sobel Test"

docs.title: 5. Sync Drafts
docs.text:
Push a vignette or RMarkdown file to 02_Drafts for prose editing in Obsidian.

obs r-dev draft vignettes/intro.Rmd

docs.title: 6. Unlink a Project
docs.text:
Remove the R project mapping when you're done.

cd ~/projects/RMediation
obs r-dev unlink

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use obs list to see all your R project mappings at a glance
  • Use --verbose flag to debug mapping issues: obs --verbose r-dev log plot.png
  • The mapping file is plain JSON, you can edit ~/.config/obs/project_map.json directly if needed

docs.title: v2.0 Knowledge Graph Features
docs.text: The v2.0 release transforms obs into an intelligent knowledge management system with powerful graph analysis capabilities.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
v2.0 adds a Python-powered backend that:

  • Scans your Obsidian vaults and extracts all metadata
  • Analyzes the knowledge graph structure
  • Calculates importance metrics for every note
  • Detects orphans, hubs, and broken links
  • Tracks vault statistics over time

All data is stored locally in a SQLite database at ~/.config/obs/vault_db.sqlite.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
# Install Python dependencies
pip3 install python-frontmatter mistune PyYAML networkx

# Initialize database (creates ~/.config/obs/vault_db.sqlite)
python3 src/python/obs_cli.py db init

docs.title: Basic Workflow
docs.text:
# 1. Discover vaults in a directory
obs discover ~/Documents -v

# 2. Scan and analyze a vault
obs discover ~/Documents --scan -v

# 3. View results
obs vaults          # List all vaults
obs stats           # Global statistics
obs stats <id>      # Vault-specific stats

# 4. Analyze graph
obs analyze <vault> -v

docs.title: obs discover [path]
docs.text:
Find Obsidian vaults in a directory tree.

# Find vaults (no scanning)
obs discover ~/Documents -v

# Find and scan automatically
obs discover ~/Documents --scan -v

How it works: Searches for directories containing .obsidian folders.

docs.title: obs analyze <vault>
docs.text:
Analyze vault knowledge graph and calculate metrics. Accepts vault name or ID prefix.

# Analyze by name
obs analyze Knowledge_Base -v

# Or by ID prefix (from obs vaults output)
obs analyze a812 -v

Metrics calculated: - PageRank (importance score) - In/out degree (connection counts) - Betweenness centrality - Closeness centrality - Clustering coefficient

docs.title: Markdown Parsing
docs.text:
Extracts comprehensive metadata from every note:

  • Frontmatter: YAML metadata
  • Title: From frontmatter, first H1, or filename
  • Wikilinks: [[target]] and [[target|display]]
  • Tags: Both #tag and #nested/tag
  • Timestamps: Created and modified dates
  • Statistics: Word count, character count

docs.title: Link Resolution
docs.text:
Intelligently resolves wikilinks to actual notes:

  1. Exact path match
  2. Path without .md extension
  3. Relative path from source note
  4. Filename-only match

Broken links are detected and tracked in the database.

docs.title: PageRank
docs.text: Importance score based on link structure (like Google's algorithm). Notes that are linked to by important notes get higher scores.

docs.title: Degree Centrality
docs.text:
• In-degree: How many notes link to this one
  • Out-degree: How many notes this one links to

docs.title: Betweenness Centrality
docs.text: How often a note appears on the shortest path between other notes. High betweenness = bridge between topics.

docs.title: Closeness Centrality
docs.text: Average distance to all other notes in the graph. High closeness = well-connected.

docs.title: Clustering Coefficient
docs.text: How connected a note's neighbors are to each other. High clustering = tightly-knit topic cluster.

docs.title: Orphaned Notes
docs.text:
Notes with no incoming or outgoing links. These might need better integration into your knowledge graph.

obs stats <vault>

Look for "Orphaned notes" count.

docs.title: Hub Notes
docs.text:
Notes with more than 10 total connections (in + out). These are central to your knowledge base.

obs analyze <vault> -v

Shows top 5 hub notes with connection counts.

docs.title: Broken Links
docs.text:
Wikilinks that don't resolve to any note. Might be typos or deleted notes.

obs stats <vault>

Shows broken link count and sources.

docs.title: Database Schema
docs.text: The SQLite database contains:

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
• vaults: Vault metadata
  • notes: All notes with content hashes
  • links: Wikilink relationships
  • tags: Tag definitions
  • note_tags: Many-to-many tag associations
  • graph_metrics: Calculated metrics
  • scan_history: Scan tracking

docs.title: Views
docs.text:
• orphaned_notes: Notes with no links
  • hub_notes: Highly connected notes (>10 links)
  • broken_links: Unresolved wikilinks

docs.title: Auto-Updates
docs.text: Triggers automatically update: - Vault note counts - Tag usage counts - Graph in/out degrees

docs.title: 1. Vault Health Check
docs.text:
# Scan vault
obs discover ~/Documents/Obsidian/MyVault --scan -v

# Get vault ID
obs vaults

# Check stats
obs stats <vault>

Look for: - High orphan count → Need more linking - Many broken links → Clean up or update links - Low density → Isolated clusters

docs.title: 2. Find Important Notes
docs.text:
# Analyze graph
obs analyze <vault> -v

Top hub notes are your most connected concepts. Consider: - Adding more detail to these notes - Breaking them into sub-topics if too large - Ensuring they're well-maintained

docs.title: 3. Discover Gaps
docs.text: Notes with high betweenness but low in-degree are bridges between topics but not well-documented themselves. Great candidates for expansion.

docs.title: 4. Track Over Time
docs.text:
Re-scan regularly and compare: 

# Scan weekly
obs discover ~/Documents --scan -v

# Track stats
obs stats <vault>

Watch for: - Growing orphan count - Increasing broken links - Changing hub notes

docs.title: Scanning Speed
docs.text:
• ~100 notes/second on modern hardware
  • 1,000 note vault: ~10 seconds
  • 10,000 note vault: ~2 minutes

docs.title: Analysis Speed
docs.text:
• Link resolution: O(n) with caching
  • PageRank: O(n × iterations)
  • Centrality: O(n²) for betweenness/closeness

Large vaults (>10k notes) may take a few minutes for full analysis.

docs.title: Memory Usage
docs.text:
• Database: ~1KB per note
  • NetworkX graph: ~100 bytes per edge
  • 10,000 note vault with 50,000 links: ~100MB RAM

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Version: 3.0.0

Obsidian CLI Ops follows a clean three-layer architecture with an optional AI feature layer.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Presentation (CLI)  -->  Application (Core Logic)  -->  Data (DB/Files)
                              |
                         AI Features (optional)

Goals: Code reusability, testability, flexibility, maintainability.

docs.title: Layer Diagram
docs.text:
Presentation Layer
  ZSH CLI (obs.zsh, 386 lines) --> Python CLI (obs_cli.py)

Application Layer (Core)
  VaultManager (311 lines)    GraphAnalyzer (311 lines)
  Domain Models (237 lines)   Custom Exceptions

AI Features Layer (Optional)
  AIRouter (312 lines)        Features (~960 lines)
  5 Providers                 ObsidianBridge (123 lines)

Data Layer
  DatabaseManager (469 lines) VaultScanner (373 lines)
  GraphBuilder (307 lines)    SQLite Database

docs.title: Zero Duplication
docs.text:
Business logic lives in the Core layer only. The CLI is a thin presentation layer that formats output.

# Core layer (shared logic)
class VaultManager:
    def scan_vault(self, path: str) -> ScanResult:
        # Business logic once
        ...

# CLI (presentation only)
def scan_command(args):
    result = vault_manager.scan_vault(args.path)
    print(f"Scanned {result.notes_scanned} notes")  # Formatting

docs.title: Domain Models
docs.text:
Type-safe dataclasses for all business entities:

  • Vault, Note, ScanResult, GraphMetrics, VaultStats
  • AI models: AnalysisResult, ComparisonResult, SimilarNote

All models have from_db_row(), to_dict(), and to_json() methods.

docs.title: AI Provider Architecture
docs.text:
5 providers with automatic fallback routing:

gemini-api > anthropic-api > ollama > gemini-cli > claude-cli
  • Providers implement a common AIProvider interface
  • All return the same dataclass types (no provider-specific returns)
  • Embedding cache in SQLite with mtime invalidation
  • ObsidianBridge uses the Null Object pattern (returns empty results when CLI unavailable)

docs.title: Scanning a Vault
docs.text:
User --> obs scan /vault
  --> ZSH CLI (dispatcher)
    --> Python CLI (parse args)
      --> VaultManager.scan_vault()
        --> VaultScanner.scan_vault()
          --> DatabaseManager (INSERT notes, links, tags)
            --> SQLite

docs.title: AI Feature (suggest-links)
docs.text:
User --> obs ai suggest-links note-1
  --> Python CLI
    --> suggest_links(note_id, db)
      --> Get note embedding (cached in note_embeddings table)
      --> Compare to all candidates
      --> Exclude existing links
      --> Return top-N suggestions

    ~/Documents/TestVault-$size \
    --notes $notes --density $density --tags $tags

obs supports multiple AI providers for advanced vault analysis:

  3. Let you choose a default provider
  4. Test the connection

docs.title: Step 5: Find Similar Notes
docs.text:
Find notes that are semantically similar to a given note:

obs ai similar <note_id>
Finding note IDs

Note IDs come from the database. Use obs stats --vault MyVault with verbose mode, or query the database directly.

How it works:

  1. Generates embeddings (vector representations) for your notes
  2. Compares using cosine similarity
  3. Returns the most similar notes ranked by score

Use cases:

  • Discover related notes you forgot about
  • Find candidates for merging or cross-linking
  • Identify knowledge clusters

docs.text:

obs ai analyze <note_id>

  2. "Python Setup" ↔ "Setting Up Python" (similarity: 0.85)

  • Merge confirmed duplicates using Obsidian's note merge
  • Differentiate near-duplicates by adding unique content

  2. [[Algorithms]] (65%)

obs ai gaps MyVault

Different providers excel at different tasks:

Provider Speed Quality Privacy Cost gemini-api Fast High Cloud API key gemini-cli Medium High Cloud Free claude-cli Medium Highest Cloud Free ollama Slow Good Local Free

docs.text:

Time: ~15 minutes | Level: Intermediate | Steps: 9

Prerequisites: Complete Getting Started (vault scanned)

docs.title: Step 1: What is Graph Analysis?
docs.text:
Your Obsidian vault is a graph — notes are nodes, wikilinks are edges. Graph analysis reveals the structure of your knowledge:

  • Hub notes — highly connected, central to your thinking
  • Orphan notes — isolated, may need integration
  • Clusters — groups of tightly related notes
  • Broken links — wikilinks pointing to non-existent notes

docs.title: Step 2: Run Graph Analysis
docs.text:
Analyze a vault by name or ID prefix:

obs analyze MyVault

Expected output:

📊 Graph Analysis: MyVault
   Notes: 142
   Links: 387
   Density: 0.0193
   Clusters: 8
Verbose mode

Add -v for detailed output including top hub notes and orphan counts: 

obs analyze MyVault -v

docs.title: Step 3: Understand Graph Density
docs.text:
Density measures how interconnected your vault is, from 0.0 (no links) to 1.0 (every note links to every other).

Density Interpretation < 0.01 Sparse — many isolated notes 0.01–0.05 Typical — healthy vault 0.05–0.10 Dense — well-connected > 0.10 Very dense — may have over-linking

Most Obsidian vaults fall in the 0.01–0.05 range.

docs.title: Step 4: Find Hub Notes
docs.text:
Hub notes are the most connected in your vault — they're the backbone of your knowledge graph.

obs analyze MyVault -v

Look for the "Top Hub Notes" section:

  🌟 Top Hub Notes:
    • MOC - Machine Learning (47 connections)
    • Index - Projects (32 connections)
    • Daily Notes Overview (28 connections)
    • Research Methods (21 connections)
    • Tool Comparisons (18 connections)

What to do with hubs:

  • Review them regularly — they influence many notes
  • Consider splitting hubs with 50+ connections
  • Hubs are great starting points for new readers

docs.title: Step 5: Find Orphaned Notes
docs.text:
Orphaned notes have no incoming or outgoing links. They're invisible to graph navigation.

obs stats --vault MyVault

Check the "Orphaned" count in Graph Health:

  Graph Health
    Orphaned: 12

What to do with orphans:

  • Link them to relevant hub notes or MOCs (Maps of Content)
  • Some orphans are fine (daily notes, templates)
  • High orphan count (>20%) suggests poor linking habits

docs.title: Step 6: Detect Broken Links
docs.text:
Broken links are wikilinks ([[target]]) that don't resolve to any existing note.

obs stats --vault MyVault

Check the "Broken Links" count:

  Graph Health
    Broken Links: 3

Common causes:

  • Renamed notes without updating links
  • Deleted notes that were referenced
  • Typos in wikilink targets

Fix: Create the missing notes, or update the links to point to correct targets.

docs.title: Step 7: Understand Clusters
docs.text:
Clusters are groups of notes that are more connected to each other than to the rest of the vault. They often represent topic areas.

The "Clusters" count in your analysis output tells you how many distinct communities exist:

   Clusters: 8

Interpreting clusters:

  • Each cluster typically represents a topic or project
  • Very few clusters (1-2) might mean your vault lacks structure
  • Many small clusters might mean topics aren't cross-linked enough

docs.title: Step 8: Track Changes Over Time
docs.text:
Re-scan and re-analyze periodically to track how your vault evolves:

# Re-scan to pick up new notes and links
obs scan /path/to/vault

# Re-analyze
obs analyze MyVault -v

Watch for:

  • Orphan count increasing — linking habits may be slipping
  • Broken links growing — maintenance needed
  • Density increasing — vault is becoming better connected
  • New clusters forming — your knowledge is expanding
